### S1-14 – Health and safety metrics

Air France-KLM monitors workplace accidents through indicators covering the number of accidents, fatalities, accident frequency and accident severity. Reporting arrangements and definitions differ between France and the Netherlands, which limits comparability and aggregation at Group level. In particular, significant differences exist in the criteria used to define work-related accidents in the two countries.

For 2019, the Corporate Sustainability Tracker records **five fatalities resulting from work-related injuries and work-related ill health** under each of the following classifications:

- employees within the own-workforce category: **5**;
- non-employees within the own-workforce category: **5**;
- employees within the category of other workers working on the undertaking’s sites: **5**; and
- non-employees within the category of other workers working on the undertaking’s sites: **5**.

These source classifications overlap and do not provide sufficient information to determine whether they represent separate incidents or the same fatalities reported under multiple workforce categories. Accordingly, the values have not been aggregated. The evidence also does not distinguish fatalities caused by work-related injuries from those caused by work-related ill health. In 2018, the corresponding fatality indicators available for employees and non-employees were zero.

The Group has progressively developed the coverage of its health and safety reporting. Frequency and severity rates for work-related accidents in Air France subsidiaries were reported for the first time in 2018; these subsidiaries represented approximately 7% of Group headcount. In preceding years, these indicators had not been reported because no centralised reporting procedure was in place. Measures had been identified to progressively expand indicator reporting.

For KLM subsidiaries, reporting coverage increased from 85% in 2017 to 87% in 2018. In 2018, KLM subsidiaries recorded 75 workplace accidents, compared with 53 in 2017. The frequency rate increased from 5.26 to 6.56, while the severity rate decreased from 0.42 to 0.35. No fatal workplace accidents were recorded in either year.

Frequency and severity rates are calculated for all staff using theoretically worked hours. For KLM and its subsidiaries, days lost due to work-related accidents are tracked using figures declared by KLM entities in the Netherlands. No consolidated 2019 figures for total recordable accidents, frequency rate, severity rate, days lost, occupational ill-health cases or health and safety management-system coverage are available in the evidence. The evidence also does not specify a quantitative health and safety target or a Group-level governance body responsible for these metrics.

## G1-2 – Management of relationships with suppliers

Air France-KLM seeks to integrate corporate social responsibility principles throughout its supplier relationships, with particular emphasis on ethical, social and environmental risks. The Group’s commitments to environmental protection, social equity, local development and fair stakeholder practices are set out in its Corporate Social Responsibility Statement. In its relationships with suppliers and subcontractors worldwide, the Group expects compliance with applicable laws, fundamental social rights and environmental protection requirements. This includes respect for human rights and opposition to child labour and all forms of forced or compulsory labour.

The joint Air France-KLM Procurement function is responsible for embedding these principles in procurement processes. A supplier selection process has been implemented in response to duty-of-vigilance requirements. Environmental and occupational health and safety obligations are incorporated into relevant product or service specifications. Suppliers are also invited to sign the Group’s Sustainable Development Charter, which is based on the principles of the United Nations Global Compact.

The proportion of suppliers having signed the Sustainable Development Charter is monitored annually. In 2018, 67% of suppliers had signed the Charter, against a target of 70% for 2019. The evidence available for this disclosure does not provide the year-end 2019 achievement against that target.

Buyer awareness and conduct support the implementation of the Group’s supplier-management approach. Procurement provides awareness training on ethical, social and environmental risks. Buyers are encouraged to sign a Code of Ethics setting out the rules applicable when dealing with suppliers. The Code of Ethics, Sustainable Development Charter and Code of Conduct are made available through the Procurement website. An internal responsible-purchasing process provides buyers with information on environmental good practices, training and seminars to strengthen their ability to consider environmental and social criteria in purchasing decisions. The Air France and KLM CSR departments also participate with Procurement in responsible-purchasing working groups organised by AFNOR and other bodies.

For strategic suppliers, the Supplier Relations Management programme supports long-term relationships and enables corporate social responsibility matters to be addressed as part of ongoing dialogue. Suppliers are included following segmentation and qualification, in close coordination with the relevant businesses.

The Group also develops an annual action plan for relationships with SMEs, midcaps, start-ups and very small businesses. Measures pursued in 2018 included reducing payment terms through the extension of the Tradeshift buyer-supplier platform and facilitating collaboration with start-ups through a “start-up Kit”, proof-of-concept trials and the Digital Factory. These actions contributed to Air France attaining the SME Pact partner committee’s “A” level of excellence, providing a basis for continued attention to fair and effective supplier relationships in 2019.

### S1-5 – Targets related to own-workforce impacts, risks and opportunities

Air France-KLM considers safeguarding employee health and safety a major priority and an area in which there can be no compromise. The Group’s approach is based on evaluating and analysing existing and emerging occupational risks and deploying appropriate prevention measures. Air France’s proactive Health and Safety Policy is supported by a consolidated Health and Safety Manual, relevant key performance indicators and an Integrated Management System connecting workplace health and safety with other risk-management and continuous-improvement processes.

Occupational-accident reduction objectives are incorporated into management arrangements. Through target-based contracts, Executive Vice-Presidents formalise commitments to reducing occupational accidents by means of prevention plans. These commitments reflect the specific circumstances of the activities concerned while remaining consistent with the Company’s principal objectives. More broadly, annual target-based contracts are signed between the relevant Executive Vice-President or Vice-President and the CEO, monitored twice annually, and used to establish collective and individual targets. Progress is reported to Management Committees, reviewed through regular strategic updates by the Air France Executive Committee and considered through a dedicated Health and Safety Management Review.

The indicators used to monitor workforce impacts include absenteeism due to illness and workplace accidents, the frequency rate of workplace accidents with lost time, accident severity, training hours per employee, employees with disabilities, gender representation and signed collective agreements. Social reporting covers Air France in France, HOP!, KLM in the Netherlands and KLM Catering Services. Differences between French and Dutch definitions of work-related accidents may affect comparability and are considered when interpreting results.

For 2019, five employee fatalities were reported under both the combined indicator for work-related injuries and work-related ill health and the indicator for work-related injuries. Five fatalities were also reported for non-employees under the combined injury and ill-health indicator. This compares with zero fatalities reported in 2018 for employees and non-employees under the combined indicator, and zero employee fatalities from work-related injuries. The available information does not provide a disaggregation that would permit the combined 2019 employee and non-employee figures to be added without possible double counting.

Air France’s Diversity Charter provides a formal commitment to better reflect the diversity of the French population within its workforce and to combat all forms of discrimination. However, no quantified, time-bound diversity target, baseline or target year was reported for 2019. Similarly, although accident-reduction commitments form part of management contracts, no consolidated Group-level numerical health and safety target or defined 2019 target threshold was disclosed. Accordingly, performance is monitored through management reviews and workforce indicators, but progress against a quantified S1-5 target cannot be stated for the reporting year.

### S1-4 — Actions, resources and effectiveness related to own workforce

Air France-KLM’s workforce actions focus on occupational health and safety, sustainable employability, skills development and equal opportunities. The Group monitors social indicators covering workforce composition by age, gender and geography; women among the top 10% of management levels; recruitment and departures; sickness and workplace-accident absenteeism; accident frequency and severity; training hours; employees with disabilities; and collective agreements.

At KLM, preventive action is structured through occupational-safety policies, continuous Risk Assessment & Evaluation, the integration of occupational requirements into audits and division-level goal-setting. This approach was informed by benchmarking with other airlines and comparable Dutch companies. Ground-staff risks identified as high include collisions with equipment and slips and trips, for which mitigating actions had been initiated. In 2018, the KLM Board endorsed the “KLM 100 years and beyond veilig en gezond (safe and sound)” programme, aimed at strengthening prevention and improving sustainable employability. KLM also continued investing in improved working conditions and healthy lifestyles, supported by initiatives designed to provide an integrated framework through which the organisation and employees can contribute to health, employability, productivity and operational performance.

Skills development remained a significant component of workforce-related resources. At Air France, 95% of employees benefited from training in 2018. Access was broadened through My Learning self-service modules, Massive Open Online Courses, Manager Cafés and dedicated days for HR and manager networks. Flight Safety Training comprised 1,500 courses and 41,000 training days. A new knowledge-development tool was used by 95% of the relevant crew population, representing approximately 9,800 employees.

Effectiveness is assessed through health and safety outcomes, training participation and employee-engagement results, including the Employee Promoter Score. For 2019, five employee fatalities were reported under the indicator covering work-related injuries and work-related ill health; the reported number of employee fatalities resulting specifically from work-related injuries was also five. This compares with zero fatalities reported under both corresponding indicators in 2018. Separately, five fatalities were reported for non-employees under the combined work-related injury and ill-health indicator. These indicators are presented according to their respective reporting categories and should not be aggregated because their definitions overlap.

The social reporting perimeter used for consolidated indicators comprises Air France in France, HOP!, KLM in the Netherlands and KLM Catering Services. Reported information is supported by processes for identifying, prioritising and validating principal risks and by the monitoring of accident frequency, accident severity, absenteeism and training outcomes.

### E1-1 – Transition plan for climate change mitigation

Air France-KLM recognises that aviation contributes to climate change and has implemented a Climate Action Plan embodying the Group’s strategy for reducing its climate impact. The plan supports the Group’s low-carbon strategy across all components of its business and provides the framework through which climate-related targets and action plans are established.

The Climate Action Plan is structured around six mitigation priorities. Key levers reported include continued fleet modernisation, contributions to aeronautics research, technical and operational improvements, optimisation of flight procedures in line with recommendations from aircraft and engine manufacturers and equipment suppliers, and progress in the production and use of sustainable alternative aviation biofuels. These measures form part of the broader basket of mitigation actions deployed by the international aviation industry to reduce CO₂ emissions.

The Group’s principal near-term carbon-efficiency objective was to reduce CO₂ emissions per passenger-kilometre by 20% by 2020. For the 2019 reporting year, the reported climate-target indicators included 50.0% for the proportion of the target related to Scope 1 greenhouse gas emissions and -83.5% for the proportion related to location-based Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions, measured against base-year emissions. These indicators complement the operational carbon-intensity target, although the available information does not specify the associated base year, absolute emissions pathway or methodology for translating these percentages into the Group’s overall transition trajectory.

Fleet renewal is an important component of the plan and requires capital expenditure within the Group’s broader financial framework. Previously reported financial resources allocated to the climate action plan amounted to USD 804.9 million in 2016 and USD 2,542.7 million in 2017. Fleet capital expenditure is managed under strict capital discipline, including consideration of debt ratios and the Group’s capacity to generate positive free cash flow. No specific climate-related capital expenditure amount is reported in the available evidence for 2019.

Climate-related financial risks are incorporated into Group risk management in accordance with the requirements of Article 173 III of the French Energy Transition for Green Growth Act. Management of identified risks is integrated into the steering of business activities through common prevention methods and tools under the Group’s duty-of-vigilance approach.

For 2019, the available reporting does not establish alignment of the Climate Action Plan with a 1.5°C pathway, quantify locked-in greenhouse gas emissions, or specify time-bound milestones beyond the 2020 carbon-efficiency target. These elements therefore remain outside the scope of this disclosure.
